blueprint.speaker: A baker in a small river town, a man of long standing at his trade, awake at four in the morning and also the father of a young boy asleep upstairs.
blueprint.addressee: His own hands, addressed directly as 'you' throughout.
blueprint.situation: At four in the morning the baker descends to the bakehouse on Wendle Street. He inspects his hands (splayed thumbs, an old burn scar, flour in the creases), works the dough, anticipates the town consuming his bread by six, and recalls seeing his hands rest on the stair as if they were not his. Upstairs his son sleeps; he has meant to send the boy to school and spare him the trade, but finds the second apron already taken down from its peg.
blueprint.central_idea: A lifetime of labor can make the body an agent with habits and loyalties of its own, so that what a man thinks he intends for himself and his child may already have been decided by his hands.
blueprint.complexity: The speaker both prizes his hands (their skill, their usefulness, the honest bargain of bread over gold) and feels estranged from them (they are consumed by the town, hidden at church, resting on the stair as if not his). He wants to spare his son the trade yet discovers that he, or his hands, has already set out the boy's apron; the final line refuses to settle whether will or habit has acted.
blueprint.form_notes: Dramatic monologue in loose blank verse, five stanzas of unequal length. Apostrophe to the hands splits the speaker into two agents. Heavy use of mid-line stops and enjambment; the fourth stanza turns outward to the town and then inward to unease; the final stanza turns on 'And yet at four'.
blueprint.setting: A bakehouse below the family's living quarters on Wendle Street, in a small town, before dawn in the 19th century; lamp lit, oven holding the previous night's heat.
characters: Carter's wife, the schoolmaster, the Hollins boys (customers)

devices.quote: You wake before me, as you always do
devices.function: Addresses the hands as a separate 'you', establishing the division between the man and his hands that the poem develops.

devices.quote: the man you carry
devices.function: Reverses the expected hierarchy: the hands are the bearers and the man the burden, making the body the agent.

devices.quote: before the man you carry
devices.function: The hands acting ahead of the man anticipates the ending, in which the hands may have taken down the boy's apron.

devices.quote: as a cellar keeps its cold
devices.function: The oven holding last night's heat is likened to a cellar holding cold, conveying the bakehouse as a place with its own stored, patient character.

devices.quote: as dogs go to the hand that feeds them
devices.function: Hands going to the oven like dogs to a feeding hand conveys loyal, instinctive dependence on the work; the irony that hands go to a 'hand' deepens the sense of a split self.

devices.quote: has found his boots. The lamp is lit. The oven
devices.function: Clipped mid-line stops enact the rote, practiced sequence of the morning routine.

devices.quote: and down the stair before the man you carry
devices.function: The line runs over as the hands run ahead, delaying the surprising verb 'has found' and the reversal of agency.

devices.quote: Thumbs splayed as flat as spades
devices.function: Tool-like, deformed thumbs are set against the later 'small and unmarked' fists of the boy.

devices.quote: a white road running
devices.function: The burn scar as a road links the hands to a lived history and to the journey of the trade across the body.

devices.quote: and flour in every crease, so that at church
devices.function: Concrete tactile and visual detail of flour in the skin; the flour becomes a disguise that hides the hands from the parson.

devices.quote: a pair of gloves, and not the hands inside
devices.function: The flour that marks the hands as a baker's also conceals them; the speaker hides what defines him in the one public place he attends.

devices.quote: The dough is sullen at this hour. It sulks
devices.function: Gives the dough a reluctant human mood, making the hands' work a kind of coaxing or waking of a fellow sleeper.

devices.quote: The dough is sullen
devices.function: The word 'sullen' casts the dough as a moody child, connecting it to the sleeping boy upstairs.

devices.quote: wake it, work it, warm it
devices.function: Repeated initial w sounds mimic the rhythmic, repetitive motions of kneading.

devices.quote: No Midas, you:
devices.function: Alludes to the mythical king whose touch turned everything to gold; the hands turn things to bread instead, useful but never enriching.

devices.quote: though it has never made one baker rich
devices.function: Undercuts the claim of 'the better bargain' with wry acknowledgment of poverty.

devices.quote: By six the street will have you.
devices.function: Turns from private inspection of the hands to the town's claim on them.

devices.quote: will take you home in paper
devices.function: The hands are equated with the bread they make, carried home, broken at tables, consumed without the baker's name being spoken.

devices.quote: That is the trade.
devices.function: Short declarative sentences convey settled, unargued acceptance before the qualification 'or did not' unsettles it.

devices.quote: I did not make it, and do not mind it,
devices.function: The repeated negatives build a flat acceptance that the next line immediately revises.

devices.quote: or did not, till I saw you yesterday
devices.function: Acceptance gives way to unease at the memory of the hands resting on the stair as if they were strangers.

devices.quote: small and unmarked
devices.function: The boy's untouched fists are set against the scarred, splayed, floured hands of the father.

devices.quote: keep him from the trough
devices.function: The dough trough, earlier the site of the hands' skill, becomes the trade itself and the fate the speaker hopes to spare his son.

devices.quote: the second apron taken from its peg
devices.function: The apron taken down stands for the boy's induction into the trade, already begun before the speaker consciously chooses it.

devices.quote: and cannot say which one of us has done it
devices.function: The speaker cannot distinguish his own will from his hands' habit, leaving the question of agency unresolved.

shifts.quote: By six the street will have you.
shifts.from: private, close inspection of the hands and their work in the bakehouse
shifts.to: the town's public claim on the hands as bread consumed without acknowledgment

shifts.quote: or did not, till I saw you yesterday
shifts.to: unease that the hands have a life apart from the speaker

shifts.from: the stated intention to send the boy to school and keep him from the trade
shifts.to: the discovery that the boy's apron has already been taken down, by hands or by the man

g-p01.title: Four O'Clock, Wendle Street
g-p01.headnote: The following poem was published in 1871. The speaker, a baker, addresses his own hands.
stanzas: You wake before me, as you always do,
and down the stair before the man you carry
has found his boots. The lamp is lit. The oven
keeps last night's heat as a cellar keeps its cold,
and you go to it as dogs go to the hand that feeds them.
Let me look at you. Thumbs splayed as flat as spades
from thirty years of pressing down a seam;
across the left, a white road running
from wrist to knuckle, where the oven door
swung back the winter Lydia was born;
and flour in every crease, so that at church
I fold you under, and the parson sees
a pair of gloves, and not the hands inside.
The dough is sullen at this hour. It sulks
in the trough like something that would rather sleep,
and you go in and wake it, work it, warm it,
till it comes round and gives you back
its slow breath on the knuckles. No Midas, you:
what you touch does not turn gold. It turns to bread,
which men can eat, the better bargain,
though it has never made one baker rich.
By six the street will have you. Carter's wife,
the schoolmaster, the Hollins boys who count
their pennies twice, will take you home in paper,
break you at their tables, say the grace,
and never say your name. That is the trade.
I did not make it, and do not mind it,
or did not, till I saw you yesterday
rest flat against the stairway wall
a moment, as if you were not mine.
Upstairs the boy sleeps with his fists shut,
small and unmarked, and I have meant all week
to send him to the school at Kell's Cross
and keep him from the trough. And yet at four,
when you come down ahead of me, I find
the second apron taken from its peg,
and cannot say which one of us has done it.

characters: Agnes Rune, nineteen, raised partly on the island, now living on the mainland; sent by her grandmother to sell the family boat
Hedda Rune, Agnes's grandmother, bedridden in a mainland home, absent from the scene but directing it by letter
Osk Pell, an island neighbor in his sixties, buyer of the boat, former creditor of Agnes's grandfather
blueprint.setting: Scarrow Island, a small northern fishing island reached by ferry, late autumn in the 1950s; the shingle beach, the boat shed, the hauled-out boat Linnet; the mainland visible as a gray line across the water
blueprint.situation: Agnes arrives on the morning ferry with a pre-written bill of sale and instructions not to haggle and not to go up to the house. Pell names an absurdly low price, then reveals that Hedda set it herself to repay an old debt disguised as a sale.
blueprint.conflict: Agnes believes she is performing a plain transaction on her own authority; she discovers she is the instrument of her grandmother's arrangement with Pell, and must decide whether to obey the instruction to stay away from the house and catch the afternoon ferry.
blueprint.central_idea: Acts of settling accounts between the old are carried out through the young, who discover that what looked like their own errand was someone else's unfinished business; the recognition of being used is also a recognition of belonging.
blueprint.complexity: Hedda's manipulation is both a humiliation of Agnes and a kind of trust; Pell's acceptance of an unfair price in his favor is also an act of loyalty to a dead man and a proud woman; Agnes's final disobedience (going up to the house, missing the ferry) is simultaneously a rejection of being used and a deeper acceptance of her place in the family's accounts. The boat, sold for nothing, is worth more to everyone than its price.

devices.quote: like something that had not agreed to be walked on
devices.function: Figures the island shingle as resisting Agnes's return, establishing her estrangement and the island's indifference to her errand

devices.quote: like a scar that had decided to stay
devices.function: The replaced plank becomes a healed wound with its own will, tying the boat to family history and to the stubbornness that governs the sale

devices.quote: a face the weather had been at for sixty years
devices.function: Weather becomes an unfinished craftsman working on Pell, marking him as shaped by the island and suggesting incompleteness, the way the debt is unfinished

devices.quote: the plain thing had a hole in it
devices.function: Agnes's simple plan is figured as a leaking hull, letting cold in; links her inner disturbance to the boat and foreshadows the bailer

devices.quote: You sold a boat; you took the money
devices.function: Agnes's brisk mental script in second-person generalities exposes her wish for the errand to be impersonal, which the scene denies

devices.quote: She remembered Hedda in the stern
devices.function: Inserts the image of Hedda refusing to let the boat go anywhere before Pell explains the price, so his explanation confirms rather than surprises

devices.quote: the coin you were supposed to put in the mouth of the dead
devices.function: Charon's fee frames the sale as a passage toward death and the money as funeral payment; the inversion (the ferryman paying) captures Agnes's confusion about who is giving and who is taking

devices.quote: She wants it to look like a sale.
devices.function: The sale that Agnes came to perform is revealed as a disguise for a repayment, undercutting the title act of the passage

devices.quote: it did not change the shape of her hand
devices.function: The money's triviality is registered physically rather than announced, flattening the climax into a wry, bodily fact

devices.quote: a square, slow, salt-cured man
devices.function: Compressed sibilants give Pell a solid, deliberate sound matching his unhurried conduct

devices.quote: Never once.
devices.function: The fragment insists on Pell's lifelong exclusion from the boat, hinting at the unpaid debt before it is spoken

devices.quote: There's a bailer in the kitchen
devices.function: The bailer Hedda removed so Pell would not get it symbolizes what she withholds even while giving; carrying it to her becomes the task Agnes chooses over the one assigned

devices.quote: he did not help her, and he did not hurry
devices.function: Pell's deliberateness against Agnes's haste in city shoes defines her as the outsider and him as the island's tempo

devices.quote: Agnes had thought she was the one doing the selling.
devices.function: The sentence turns from brisk transaction to rueful recognition of being used, redirecting the passage toward Agnes's choice

devices.quote: the stones rolled the same as before
devices.function: Returns the opening image with Agnes's altered relation to it: the ground has not changed, her hurry has

devices.quote: There isn't a price to argue.
devices.function: Pell's flat refusal to bargain signals that the transaction is not economic, before he explains why

shifts.from: Agnes as brisk agent of a plain transaction
shifts.to: Agnes as instrument of her grandmother's arrangement, rueful and newly aware

shifts.quote: let the four o'clock leave without her
shifts.from: Compliance with Hedda's instructions and the plan to leave
shifts.to: Deliberate disobedience and lingering, accepting the island's slower time

blueprint.speaker: Third-person limited narrator aligned with Agnes; access to her memories and thoughts but not Pell's or Hedda's
blueprint.form_notes: Seven paragraphs of prose; clipped dialogue; one flashback paragraph; closing paragraph returns to the opening shingle image.

g-s01.headnote: The following passage is from the novel The Low Water Year (1957) by Teodora Hallsey. Agnes, nineteen, has been sent from the mainland to the island where her grandmother once lived.
paragraphs: The ferry put Agnes off at Scarrow at eleven, and she walked up from the slip with her grandmother's house key in one glove and the bill of sale, already made out, in the other. She had been told not to go up to the house. "There is nothing in it you want," Hedda had said from the bed in the mainland home, "and if you go in you will start wanting." So Agnes turned left along the shingle toward the boat shed instead, in city shoes, the stones rolling under her like something that had not agreed to be walked on.

The Linnet lay keel-down on her cradle where she had been hauled in October, and she looked smaller than Agnes remembered, the way the island did, the way the dock did; only the sky had kept its size. Someone had put a tarpaulin over her and weighted it with four stones, one at each corner, exactly. Agnes knew who. Osk Pell did everything in fours. He came down the path from his own place while she was still working the first stone loose, and he did not help her, and he did not hurry.

"You'll be Hedda's girl," he said. He was a square, slow, salt-cured man with a face the weather had been at for sixty years and had not finished. "She wrote me you were coming. She wrote me what to pay." "She told me not to argue the price." "There isn't a price to argue." He named it. It was less than her train fare had been. Agnes looked at the hull, at the strake her grandfather had replaced the summer she was nine, the new wood still a shade paler, like a scar that had decided to stay. "That boat is worth ten times that," she said. "You know it is." "I know it is."

She had come to do a plain thing. You sold a boat; you took the money; you caught the four o'clock back. Now the plain thing had a hole in it and she could feel the cold coming through. She remembered Hedda in the stern with the tiller under her arm like a parcel she had no intention of giving up, not steering so much as declining to let the boat go anywhere else. She remembered Osk Pell on the dock those summers, never once in the boat. Never once.

"Your grandfather owed me for the engine," Pell said. "Nineteen thirty-eight. He never paid it and I never asked, and your grandmother never forgot it. That's the price. She's paying the debt. She wants it to look like a sale." He took the stones off the other three corners himself now, one, two, three, setting each on the shingle as if it might be needed again. "If I'd offered her a fair price she'd have refused it. She'd have let the boat rot sooner than take money from me."

Agnes thought of the coin you were supposed to put in the mouth of the dead for the ferryman, and how the stories never said what happened if the ferryman was the one who paid. Across the water the mainland was a gray line with the home somewhere on it, a window, a bed, a woman who had arranged the whole morning from under a blanket and sent her granddaughter to stand in the wind and be the hands of it. Agnes had thought she was the one doing the selling. She signed the bill of sale on the Linnet's gunwale, pressing hard so the pencil would take on the damp paper, and Pell counted the money into her glove, and it was so little that it did not change the shape of her hand.

"Go up to the house," Pell said. "She told you not to. Go anyway. There's a bailer in the kitchen she took off the boat so I wouldn't get it. It's got her initials in it. Take it to her." Agnes did not answer. She walked back along the shingle, and the stones rolled the same as before, but she had the time now to let them, and at the turn where the path went up to the house instead of down to the slip, she stood for a while and let the four o'clock leave without her.

items.stem: The contrast between Agnes working at the stone and Pell, who "did not help her, and he did not hurry" ([[r1]]), primarily emphasizes

options.text: Agnes's eagerness to finish an errand on an island whose pace she no longer shares
options.label: correct
options.why: Agnes in city shoes hurrying to work the stone loose, set against Pell's deliberate approach, marks her as the outsider moving at mainland speed; the passage later confirms this when she lets the ferry leave and has 'the time now' to let the stones roll.

options.text: Pell's resentment toward a family that has excluded him from the boat for decades
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Pell's slowness is characteristic ('did everything in fours'), and nothing in his conduct or speech expresses resentment; he later acts with loyalty to Hedda.

options.text: Agnes's physical weakness compared with a man hardened by sixty years of weather
options.label: literal_for_figurative
options.why: Reads the scene as a test of strength; the stones are not described as heavy, and the contrast concerns tempo and manner, not capability.

options.text: Pell's refusal to acknowledge Agnes as the rightful seller of her grandmother's boat
options.label: reversal
options.why: Pell immediately recognizes her as 'Hedda's girl' and proceeds with the sale; he does not dispute her role, though he knows Hedda set the terms.

items.stem: A student claims that Hedda controls the sale despite her absence from the island. Which of the following sentences of commentary most clearly links the phrase "arranged the whole morning from under a blanket" ([[r1]]) to that claim?

options.text: The sentence pairs a verb of command with an image of confinement, showing that Hedda's authority survives the loss of her mobility.
options.label: correct
options.why: Directly connects the evidence ('arranged' against 'under a blanket') to the claim about control despite absence; the passage supports it with Hedda's letters to Pell and instructions to Agnes.

options.text: The sentence describes Hedda lying in bed at the home, which proves she is too ill to travel to the island herself to sell the boat.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Explains Hedda's absence rather than her control; it restates the circumstance without connecting to the claim's main point.

options.text: The sentence shows that Agnes resents being sent into the wind, which establishes the conflict between the two generations of the family.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Shifts focus from Hedda's control to Agnes's resentment and generational conflict, which the quoted phrase does not itself address.

options.text: The sentence uses the word 'blanket' to suggest that Hedda is hiding something from Agnes, which the reader learns is the debt owed to Pell.
options.label: lexical_trap
options.why: Over-reads 'blanket' as concealment; the text uses it for physical confinement, and the hidden debt is Pell's revelation, not the point of this phrase.

options.why: Pell's motives are unstated internally but he explains them plainly in speech; the passage does not render him untrustworthy.

options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Agnes comes to understand the instructions, and the narration treats Hedda's arrangement with rueful recognition rather than as cruelty.

evidence_quotes: It was less than her train fare had been.
"That's the price. She's paying the debt. She wants it to look like a sale."
Agnes had thought she was the one doing the selling.

items.stem: The image of the stones, which roll under Agnes "like something that had not agreed to be walked on" ([[r1]]) and later roll "the same as before" ([[r2]]), contributes to the passage mainly by

options.text: marking a change in Agnes rather than in the island, as her hurry gives way to time
options.label: correct
options.why: The ground is explicitly unchanged ('the same as before'); what differs is that Agnes 'had the time now to let them,' so the repeated image measures her altered relation to the place.

options.text: showing that the island grows more hostile to Agnes as she learns the truth about the sale
options.label: reversal
options.why: The stones do not grow more hostile; they are the same, and Agnes's response to them softens.

options.text: emphasizing that Agnes's city shoes are unsuited to the shingle and slow her progress
options.label: literal_for_figurative
options.why: The shoes are a detail of the first image only; the image's return concerns her inner state, not footwear.

options.text: suggesting that Pell has deliberately arranged the stones to make her walk difficult
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Confuses the shingle with the four tarpaulin stones; the beach stones are natural and Pell has no part in them.

items.stem: Agnes's thought of "the coin you were supposed to put in the mouth of the dead for the ferryman" ([[r1]]) frames the sale primarily as

options.text: a theft in which Pell, like the ferryman, takes payment from those who cannot refuse
options.label: reversal
options.why: Agnes notes that in this case the ferryman is the one paying; the allusion is inverted, not applied straightforwardly to Pell as taker.

options.text: a passage toward Hedda's death, with roles so inverted that Agnes cannot tell who pays whom
options.label: correct
options.why: The burial coin ties the sale to Hedda's approaching end, and the twist that the ferryman pays captures Agnes's realization that she is not the seller she thought.

options.text: a ritual that Agnes performs correctly because her grandmother has instructed her in it
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The allusion registers confusion ('the stories never said what happened'), not correct performance of a ritual.

options.text: a superstition of the island that Agnes, as a mainlander, no longer takes seriously
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The story is a classical myth, not an island custom, and Agnes's thought treats it seriously as a frame for her situation.

evidence_quotes: how the stories never said what happened if the ferryman was the one who paid

items.stem: The statement that the money "was so little that it did not change the shape of her hand" ([[r1]]) creates a tone best described as

options.text: bitter, as Agnes openly condemns Pell for exploiting her grandmother's pride
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: The sentence is flat and physical, not condemnatory; Agnes has already learned that Pell's price was Hedda's design.

options.text: dryly understated, registering the sum's insignificance as a bodily fact
options.label: correct
options.why: Rather than naming anger or disappointment, the narrator measures the money by what it fails to do to a glove, a restrained wryness characteristic of the whole passage.

options.text: tender, as Agnes recognizes the money as a token of Pell's love for her family
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The passage does not frame the money as a token of love, and Agnes's response is withholding, not tender.

options.text: triumphant, as Agnes realizes the boat has been kept from the open market
options.label: reversal
options.why: There is no triumph; Agnes has just recognized she was used, and the sentence deflates rather than elevates.

refs.quote: it did not change the shape of her hand

evidence_quotes: Pell counted the money into her glove, and it was so little that it did not change the shape of her hand
It was less than her train fare had been.

items.stem: Which of the following thesis statements offers the most defensible and specific interpretation of the passage?

options.text: Through the recurring image of the shingle and Agnes's silence at the end, the passage shows that she becomes the instrument of an old debt and, in resisting that role, discovers a claim on the island.
options.label: correct
options.why: Names specific techniques (recurring image, final silence) and a complex idea with tension (used, yet discovering belonging), both grounded in the text's opening and closing.

options.text: Through Pell's dialogue and Hedda's letters, the passage shows that older people often manipulate the young, and that such manipulation is always harmful to family relationships.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Generalizes beyond the text to 'older people' and 'always harmful'; the passage treats Hedda's arrangement with more ambivalence.

options.text: Through the description of the boat and the island, the passage shows that Agnes travels to Scarrow, sells the Linnet to Pell for a small sum, and then misses the afternoon ferry.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Summarizes plot rather than interpreting it; no claim about meaning or complexity is made.

options.text: Through the allusion to the ferryman and the sale's low price, the passage shows that Pell is the true owner of the boat and that Agnes comes to accept his superior moral claim to it.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The text never asserts Pell's ownership or moral superiority, and Agnes's final silence toward him does not signal acceptance of such a claim.

items.stem: The passage places Agnes's memory of Hedda at the tiller and of Pell "never once in the boat" ([[r1]]) before Pell's explanation of the debt. This ordering most significantly affects the reader by

options.text: making Pell's account confirm an impression already formed of Hedda's refusal to let go
options.label: correct
options.why: The flashback shows Hedda 'declining to let the boat go anywhere else' and Pell excluded; when Pell then explains she would 'let the boat rot sooner than take money,' the reader recognizes rather than learns.

options.text: creating suspense about whether Pell will reveal that he once stole the boat's engine
options.label: unsupported
options.why: No theft is suggested; the debt is for an engine Pell supplied, and the memory raises no such suspicion.

options.text: interrupting the dialogue so that Agnes's protest about the price loses its force
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The interruption deepens rather than dissipates the protest by giving it a history; her objection is not undercut.

options.text: establishing that Agnes remembers the island accurately and so can judge the fair value
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: The memory concerns relationships, not valuation; the passage has already settled that the boat is worth more than the price.

evidence_quotes: not steering so much as declining to let the boat go anywhere else
She remembered Osk Pell on the dock those summers, never once in the boat. Never once.
"She'd have let the boat rot sooner than take money from me."
